description: Belgian refugees, the 1914 Aliens Act, Kindertransport and Polish settlement after 1945.
content_html:
The First World War and Its Refugees

The outbreak of war in August 1914 immediately transformed Britain’s relationship with migrants. The Status of Aliens Act 1914 required all foreign nationals to register with police and restricted their movement. Thousands of German and Austro-Hungarian nationals already living in Britain — many of them long-term residents, some with British-born children — were interned or forced to leave. This was a sharp reversal of the relatively open Britain that had existed before 1905.

At the same time, Britain received its first mass refugee influx of the twentieth century: approximately 250,000 Belgian civilians who fled the German invasion. British public opinion was broadly sympathetic — Belgium’s fate was framed as a war of German aggression against a small neutral nation, and “poor little Belgium” became a propaganda staple. Belgians were housed across Britain, from country houses to purpose-built camps. However, by 1919 the British government was encouraging all Belgian refugees to return home, and most did.

Key Fact

In 1919, race riots broke out in several British port cities — Cardiff, Liverpool, Glasgow and South Shields — directed at Black and Asian sailors and their families. The riots followed demobilisation, when white servicemen returned to find jobs taken by Black and Asian workers recruited during the war. The violence was severe: in Cardiff, a man named Charles Wootton drowned trying to escape a mob. These events demonstrate that wartime solidarity and post-war hostility could coexist, and that the experiences of Black and Asian people in Britain were shaped by economic competition as well as racial prejudice.

Jewish Refugees in the 1930s

The rise of the Nazi regime in Germany from 1933 produced a new refugee crisis. Jews, political opponents, Roma and others faced systematic persecution, including the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 that stripped German Jews of citizenship. Initially, British policy was cautious: the Home Office limited the number of German Jews admitted, citing fears of antisemitism in Britain and concerns about economic competition during the Depression. By 1938, after Kristallnacht, the urgency became impossible to ignore.

British attitudes to Jewish refugees in the 1930s were genuinely mixed. Some charitable organisations, church groups and individuals worked hard to bring refugees to safety. Politicians including Winston Churchill argued for a more generous policy. But there were also significant barriers: government ministers feared public opposition, newspaper coverage was sometimes hostile, and the visa system remained restrictive for many desperate families. Thousands of Jews who applied for British visas were refused and later perished in the Holocaust.

After Kristallnacht, the British government agreed to a special scheme to bring Jewish children to Britain without their parents — the Kindertransport. Between December 1938 and the outbreak of war in September 1939, approximately 10,000 children arrived in Britain, placed with foster families or in hostels. Nicholas Winton privately organised the rescue of 669 children specifically from Czechoslovakia and is the most famous individual associated with the scheme.

The Kindertransport is often cited as a moment of British generosity. But historians have noted that it also reflected the limits of that generosity: adults were not included, and the scheme operated on the understanding that the children would eventually return. Most of the children’s parents perished in the Holocaust. The children themselves grew up as refugees — separated from their families, speaking accented English, and navigating a complex dual identity.

Polish Settlement After 1945

Poland’s wartime experience created another significant refugee community in Britain. Around 250,000 Polish servicemen and women had served with the Allied forces, including the famous Polish squadrons of the RAF who contributed substantially to the Battle of Britain in 1940. When the war ended and Poland came under Soviet control, many Polish veterans faced a difficult choice: return to a Communist-governed country where some were targeted for their wartime service, or remain in Britain.

The Polish Resettlement Act of 1947 offered Polish veterans and their families the right to settle in Britain. Approximately 120,000 Poles chose to remain. Their reception was mixed: trade unions feared competition for jobs, and some newspapers depicted them as economic migrants rather than war heroes. In Scotland, some communities organised protests against Polish workers in local industries. The episode illustrates that even communities with strong claims to British gratitude could face hostility in post-war conditions of economic scarcity.

Key Fact

The British Nationality Act of 1948 defined British nationality in terms that included all subjects of the British Empire and Commonwealth. This had direct consequences for post-war migration: it meant that people from the Caribbean, India, Pakistan and other Commonwealth countries had the legal right to come to Britain as British subjects. Though primarily intended to maintain Commonwealth unity, it was the legal framework that made the Windrush generation’s arrival possible — the subject of Lesson 8.

Both world wars produced internment of enemy nationals in Britain. In the First World War, around 30,000 Germans and Austro-Hungarians were interned on the Isle of Man and elsewhere; many were naturalised British subjects who had lived in England for decades. In the Second World War, the “collar the lot” policy of 1940 led to the internment of around 27,000 “enemy aliens,” including Jewish refugees who had fled Nazism — a deeply ironic consequence of war panic. The SS Arandora Star, carrying internees to Canada, was sunk by a German torpedo in July 1940, killing around 800 people, many of them Italian and German Jewish refugees.

These episodes show how the experience of migrants and ethnic minority communities was dramatically shaped by international events beyond their control. People who had built lives in Britain over decades could find themselves reclassified as enemies overnight when war broke out. Their loyalty to Britain was questioned precisely because of their foreign origins, regardless of their actual sentiments.
exam_tip_html: For questions covering the first half of the twentieth century, always be precise about which Act you are discussing: the 1905 Aliens Act, the 1914 Status of Aliens Act and the 1948 British Nationality Act each did different things. Do not confuse them. For the Kindertransport, remember the nuance: it was both an act of generosity and an illustration of limits (children only, not parents). The 1919 race riots are essential evidence that post-war Britain was not uniformly welcoming to those who had contributed to the war effort.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The First World War brought around 250,000 Belgian refugees to Britain and triggered the Status of Aliens Act 1914, which required foreign nationals to register with police and led to the internment of thousands of long-term German residents; the 1919 race riots showed that post-war economic tensions produced violence against Black and Asian sailors.
  • British attitudes to Jewish refugees in the 1930s were mixed: the Kindertransport (1938–39) brought approximately 10,000 Jewish children to safety, but the visa system remained restrictive and thousands of adults who applied for refuge were refused.
  • The Polish Resettlement Act of 1947 offered Polish veterans the right to settle in Britain, but their reception was often hostile; the British Nationality Act of 1948 simultaneously opened Britain to Commonwealth migrants, setting the stage for post-war Caribbean and South Asian migration.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Britain's treatment of Jewish refugees in the 1930s.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: The British government's visa system was restrictive (1); many German Jews who applied for entry were refused, and thousands later perished in the Holocaust (1). Feature 2: Some individuals and organisations worked to bring refugees to safety (1); Nicholas Winton privately organised the rescue of 669 Czech children in 1939 as part of the Kindertransport scheme (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why British attitudes towards refugees in the 1930s were mixed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons developed with specific evidence. Reason 1: Economic anxiety — with Britain still recovering from the Depression, some politicians and newspapers argued Jewish refugees would compete for scarce jobs; government ministers cited fears of public opposition. Reason 2: Antisemitism — documented antisemitic attitudes in parts of British society and government meant Jewish refugees were not always seen as deserving of sympathy; some newspaper coverage framed refugees as a burden. Secure: Both reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason explained. Emerging: General identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Kindertransport is considered both a humanitarian success and an illustration of the limits of British generosity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains success — approximately 10,000 children brought to safety, Nicholas Winton's private efforts, organised by charitable networks; and limits — adults were excluded, most parents perished, the scheme operated on expectation of eventual return, children grew up separated from families in complex situations. Connects this to broader government reluctance to admit more Jewish refugees. Secure: Explains both aspects with evidence. Developing: Explains one aspect well. Emerging: Describes the scheme without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which the 1914-18 war changed how Britain treated its migrant communities.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Examples: Status of Aliens Act 1914 required all foreign nationals to register with police and gave government powers of internment (1-2 marks); long-term German and Austro-Hungarian residents were interned despite decades of settlement (1 mark); 1919 race riots showed Black and Asian workers faced violence after demobilisation (1-2 marks). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that wartime Britain was hostile to all migrant communities? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument noting variation — Belgian refugees received substantial sympathy and support in 1914-18; Polish veterans were welcomed in principle via the 1947 Act; but German internees, Black and Asian workers (1919 riots), and Jewish refugees faced hostility. Argues that reception was contingent on perceived loyalty, race, and economic context rather than uniformly hostile. Engages with specific examples and any named interpretations. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from at least two communities. Developing: Some comparative points. Emerging: Descriptive. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the experience of Polish veterans after 1945 illustrates tensions in post-war British society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two tensions explained causally. Tension 1: Economic competition — trade unions feared Polish workers would undercut wages in post-war austerity conditions; despite the Polish Resettlement Act, Polish veterans faced hostility in some industries. Tension 2: Identity and loyalty — Polish veterans had strong claims to British gratitude for their wartime service (RAF Battle of Britain squadrons), yet were depicted in some press as economic migrants; this reveals how even demonstrable wartime contribution did not guarantee welcome. Secure: Two tensions explained. Developing: One tension explained. Emerging: General descriptions.

knowledge_checks.q: Approximately how many Jewish children were brought to Britain by the Kindertransport scheme between 1938 and 1939?
The 1919 race riots in Cardiff, Liverpool and other port cities were triggered primarily by what?
options: Economic competition for jobs after demobilisation

knowledge_checks.q: Nicholas Winton privately organised the rescue of _____ children from Czechoslovakia as part of the Kindertransport in 1939.
The _____ of 1947 offered Polish ex-servicemen and their families the right to settle in Britain in recognition of their wartime service.
Match each wartime act or event to what it involved.
right: Required foreign nationals to register with police; enabled internment
Brought around 10,000 Jewish children to Britain from Nazi-controlled Europe
Offered Polish veterans the right to settle in Britain after the war

glossary_terms.definition: British wartime emergency law passed in August 1914 that required all foreign nationals to register with police, restricted their movement and gave the government powers to detain or deport them.

The night of 9-10 November 1938 when Nazi-organised violence destroyed Jewish businesses, homes and synagogues across Germany and Austria, killing around 100 people and sending thousands to concentration camps.

A rescue scheme between December 1938 and September 1939 that brought approximately 10,000 predominantly Jewish children from Germany, Austria and Czechoslovakia to Britain, separating them from families who in most cases later perished.
English stockbroker (1909-2015) who privately organised the rescue of 669 children from Czechoslovakia via Kindertransport in 1939, actions kept secret for fifty years.
A 1947 British law that offered Polish ex-servicemen and their families the right to settle in Britain and receive assistance to integrate into civilian life, in recognition of their wartime service.

The 1948 law that defined British nationality, granting citizenship to all subjects of the British Empire and Commonwealth — a decision that opened the door to post-war Caribbean and Asian immigration.
